metadata.description: Master Double Sleeve Guard Bottom in BJJ. Control-focused open guard with sleeve grips. Learn sweeps, transitions, and guard retention with 65% advanced success rates.

overview:
Double Sleeve Guard Bottom is a fundamental open guard position where the bottom practitioner controls both of the opponent's sleeves while maintaining distance with their feet on the hips or biceps. This position provides excellent control over the opponent's upper body, preventing them from establishing grips or initiating passing sequences while setting up numerous sweep and transition opportunities. The position is particularly effective in gi jiu-jitsu, where the sleeve grips create a strong connection that can be used to manipulate the opponent's posture and balance.

Double Sleeve Guard is characterized by its emphasis on grip fighting dominance and distance management. By controlling both sleeves, the bottom player neutralizes the opponent's ability to grip the pants or control the legs, forcing them into a defensive posture. This guard excels at creating off-balancing opportunities and can transition seamlessly into more specialized guards like Spider Guard, Lasso Guard, or De La Riva Guard. The position requires good hip mobility and grip strength but offers a high return on investment for practitioners who develop proficiency with the fundamental sweeps and transitions available from this control position.
state_invariants: Bottom practitioner controls both of opponent's sleeves with firm grips at or near the cuffs, maintaining constant tension to prevent opponent from breaking grips or establishing their own control
Bottom practitioner's hips are mobile and off the mat, with feet actively posted on opponent's hips, biceps, or shoulders to maintain distance and prevent opponent from closing the gap
Opponent is on their knees or standing, unable to establish controlling grips on bottom player's pants or belt due to sleeve control, with their upper body posture being constantly manipulated
Bottom practitioner's shoulders remain on the mat with head neutral or slightly lifted to maintain visual contact with opponent's movements and maintain proper spinal alignment
Distance is maintained between bottom player's torso and top player through active foot pressure, preventing top player from establishing chest-to-chest pressure or smash passing positions
prerequisites: Opponent is in open guard top position on their knees or standing
Bottom practitioner has established grips on both of opponent's sleeves
Sufficient distance exists between bottom and top player to extend legs
Bottom practitioner's guard has not been passed and they maintain hip mobility
Opponent has not yet established dominant grips on pants or belt
key_principles: Maintain constant tension on both sleeve grips to prevent opponent from breaking grips and establishing their own control system
Use feet actively to push and pull opponent's body, creating off-balancing opportunities and preventing them from settling their weight
Keep hips mobile and ready to follow opponent's movements, adjusting foot placement as they attempt to change angles
Break opponent's posture by pulling sleeves while pushing with feet, creating a concave bend in their spine that compromises their base
Transition grips and foot placement fluidly to prevent opponent from anticipating and countering sweep attempts
Maintain visual contact with opponent and read their weight distribution to time sweeps and transitions optimally
Use the guard to control tempo and prevent opponent from initiating their passing game

Opponent stands up to break grips or create pressure

decision_tree.condition: If opponent maintains strong upright posture and attempts to break grips by pulling arms back
If opponent leans forward with weight attempting to break grips and establish chest pressure
If opponent attempts to circle or step to one side to initiate passing sequence
If opponent successfully breaks one sleeve grip and establishes pants grip

common_errors.error: Releasing tension on sleeve grips, allowing opponent to break grips easily
common_errors.consequence: Opponent establishes their own grips on pants or belt and initiates passing sequence with dominant control
common_errors.correction: Maintain constant pulling tension on both sleeves, using bicep curl motion and keeping elbows tight to body

common_errors.error: Allowing feet to rest passively on opponent's hips without active pushing
common_errors.consequence: Opponent closes distance and establishes smash passing pressure, collapsing the guard structure
common_errors.correction: Actively push with balls of feet, extending legs to create and maintain distance while adjusting pressure based on opponent's movements

common_errors.error: Keeping hips flat on mat instead of mobile and ready to move
common_errors.consequence: Unable to follow opponent's circling movements, making sweeps ineffective and allowing easy passing
common_errors.correction: Keep hips elevated slightly off mat, ready to pivot and follow opponent's direction changes

common_errors.error: Gripping too high on opponent's sleeves near the shoulders instead of at the cuffs
common_errors.consequence: Opponent has greater range of motion and can use leverage to break grips more easily
common_errors.correction: Establish grips at or near the cuffs where opponent has minimal leverage and maximum control can be maintained

common_errors.error: Attempting sweeps without first breaking opponent's posture and balance
common_errors.consequence: Sweeps fail as opponent maintains strong base and can simply step through or around sweep attempts
common_errors.correction: First use push-pull dynamics to break posture, then time sweep when opponent is off-balance

common_errors.error: Failing to transition grips when opponent adjusts position
common_errors.consequence: Opponent creates angles for passing that cannot be controlled with static double sleeve grips
common_errors.correction: Be ready to transition one sleeve grip to lasso, spider, or collar grip as opponent moves

training_drills.name: Double Sleeve Grip Retention Drill
training_drills.description: Partner attempts to break both sleeve grips using various methods while bottom player maintains grips for 2-minute rounds. Focus on grip strength, frame integrity, and re-establishing grips quickly if broken. Partner should use realistic grip breaking strategies including posting, pulling back, and circling.

training_drills.name: Sweep Chain Flow Drill
training_drills.description: From double sleeve guard, practice flowing between scissor sweep, flower sweep, and pendulum sweep based on partner's resistance. Partner provides progressive resistance, allowing successful sweeps initially then increasing difficulty. Emphasize smooth transitions between sweep options and reading partner's weight distribution.

training_drills.name: Distance Management Drill
training_drills.description: Maintain double sleeve control while partner attempts to close distance and establish chest pressure. Bottom player must use feet to maintain optimal distance, adjusting foot placement between hips, biceps, and shoulders as needed. Focus on active leg extension and hip mobility to prevent opponent from collapsing guard.

training_drills.name: Guard Transition Drill
training_drills.description: Start from double sleeve guard and transition to spider guard, lasso guard, or De La Riva guard based on partner's movement. Partner walks around attempting to pass while bottom player adjusts grips and foot placement to transition between guard types. Emphasize maintaining control throughout transitions.

expert_insights.danaher: Double sleeve guard represents one of the most fundamental control systems in gi jiu-jitsu, embodying the principle of controlling the most dangerous weapons first. By controlling both sleeves, you neutralize your opponent's primary means of establishing grips and initiating their offense. The position is built on the biomechanical reality that human beings cannot effectively attack without the use of their hands, and by denying them hand placement, you force them into a defensive posture from what should be their offensive position. The key to success in this guard is understanding that your sleeve grips must work in concert with your leg frames - the grips control their upper body while your legs control distance and create the leverage necessary for sweeps. When executing techniques from this position, focus on the push-pull dynamic: pull with your hands while pushing with your feet to break their posture and create the off-balancing necessary for high-percentage sweeps.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: In competition, double sleeve guard is my go-to position when I need to slow down an aggressive passer and set up my game on my terms. The beauty of this guard is that it's extremely difficult for opponents to pass if you maintain proper tension and distance - they literally cannot grip your pants or establish control points without first dealing with your sleeve control. I use this position to control the pace of the match and force opponents into positions where I can execute my highest percentage sweeps. The scissor sweep and flower sweep from double sleeve are money techniques that I hit constantly in competition because they work at the highest levels when timed correctly. The key is being patient and waiting for your opponent to make a mistake in their posture or base before committing to the sweep. Also, don't be married to the position - be ready to transition to spider or lasso when your opponent adjusts, because the best guard players are constantly flowing between related positions based on their opponent's reactions.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: Double sleeve guard is fundamental, but a lot of people sleep on how dynamic and creative you can be from here. At 10th Planet, we use double sleeve as a launching pad for all kinds of transitions - you can hit the classic sweeps everyone knows, but you can also set up rubber guard entries, triangle setups, and even back takes if you're creative with your grip transitions. The thing people don't realize is that when you control both sleeves, you're not just preventing their grips - you're controlling their entire upper body structure, which opens up opportunities for unorthodox attacks. I like to use double sleeve to set up omoplata entries by breaking their posture down first, then swimming one leg over the shoulder. Also, if you're in no-gi and can't get the sleeve grips, the same concepts apply to wrist control - control both wrists and use your feet to create distance, and you've got the same offensive opportunities. The key is staying creative and not just defaulting to the basic sweeps everyone expects. Mix in some unusual transitions and you'll keep opponents guessing.

metadata.description: Master Double Sleeve Guard in BJJ. Complete guide covering grips, sweeps, and transitions. Fundamental guard position with 60% retention rate for intermediates.

overview:
Double Sleeve Guard is a fundamental open guard position where the bottom practitioner controls both of the opponent's sleeves while maintaining distance with the feet. This position creates a strong defensive frame that prevents the opponent from establishing effective grips or initiating passing sequences. The position is characterized by maintaining tension on both sleeves while using the legs and hips to manage distance and create angles for attacks.

Double Sleeve Guard serves as an excellent platform for developing grip fighting skills and understanding distance management principles. By controlling both sleeves, the guard player neutralizes many common passing attempts while setting up sweeps and transitions to more offensive positions. The position requires constant movement and angle adjustment to prevent the opponent from breaking grips or establishing their own control points.

This guard position is particularly effective in gi competition and serves as a gateway to more advanced guard variations. The skills developed in Double Sleeve Guard—grip fighting, distance management, and hip movement—transfer directly to Spider Guard, Collar Sleeve Guard, and other open guard systems. Understanding Double Sleeve Guard provides practitioners with a solid foundation for developing a comprehensive open guard game.
state_invariants: Both hands maintain firm grip on opponent's sleeves at or near the wrists, creating bilateral control that prevents their hand fighting and grip establishment
Hips remain mobile and off the mat with weight distributed through shoulders and upper back, allowing dynamic repositioning and angle creation
Feet positioned on opponent's hips, biceps, or in active pushing/pulling motion against their torso to manage distance and prevent forward pressure
Spine maintains slight curve with shoulders anchored to mat while hips elevate, creating structural frame that absorbs and redirects opponent's pressure
Constant tension maintained on sleeves with elbows tucked to sides, preventing opponent from posting hands or establishing grips on legs or belt

Opponent in standing or combat base position at appropriate distance
Ability to maintain hip mobility and elevate lower body off mat
Understanding of basic open guard distance management principles
Sufficient grip strength to maintain bilateral sleeve control under pressure
key_principles: Maintain constant tension on both sleeves with elbows tight to body to prevent opponent from recovering posture or establishing grips
Use feet actively to push and pull on opponent's body, creating off-balancing opportunities and preventing static positioning
Keep hips mobile and elevated to adjust angles and distance, never allowing them to remain flat on mat
Create extension and compression cycles by pushing opponent away then pulling them forward, disrupting their balance and base
Break opponent's posture by pulling sleeves down and across their centerline while elevating hips to create sweeping angles
Transition grips and foot positions fluidly to adapt to opponent's movement and set up attacks
Maintain connection through feet on hips or biceps to feel opponent's weight distribution and anticipate their movements

common_errors.error: Allowing hips to remain flat on mat without elevation or movement
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can easily drive forward and establish pressure passing positions, nullifying distance management benefits
common_errors.correction: Constantly elevate hips and shift angles, using shoulders as pivot point to create dynamic positioning

common_errors.error: Gripping sleeves too high near elbows instead of at wrists
common_errors.consequence: Opponent retains significant arm mobility and can still establish grips or post hands effectively
common_errors.correction: Secure grips at or just above wrists to maximize control and limit opponent's hand usage

common_errors.error: Maintaining static foot positioning without active pushing or pulling
common_errors.consequence: Guard becomes passive and easy to pass, with no off-balancing or sweeping opportunities created
common_errors.correction: Use feet in constant push-pull cycles on hips, biceps, or chest to disrupt opponent's balance and create angles

common_errors.error: Allowing elbows to flare out away from body while maintaining sleeve grips
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can circle arms around outside and establish underhooks or belt grips, compromising guard
common_errors.correction: Keep elbows tight to ribs with forearms creating protective frame while maintaining sleeve tension

common_errors.error: Failing to transition or attack when opponent's base is compromised
common_errors.consequence: Missed opportunities to sweep or submit, allowing opponent to recover posture and restart passing attempts
common_errors.correction: Immediately capitalize on any forward lean, weight shift, or base narrowing with appropriate sweep or submission

common_errors.error: Gripping with thumb-in grip instead of four-fingers or pistol grip
common_errors.consequence: Easier for opponent to break grips with spinning or pulling motions, weakening entire guard structure
common_errors.correction: Use four-fingers or pistol grip configuration for maximum grip strength and retention under pressure

training_drills.name: Grip Retention Drill
training_drills.description: Partner establishes Double Sleeve Guard while opponent attempts to break grips using various methods (spinning, pulling, posting). Focus on maintaining grips while adjusting hip position and foot placement. Work 2-minute rounds with role switching.

training_drills.name: Extension-Compression Cycle Flow
training_drills.description: From Double Sleeve Guard, practice rhythmic extension (pushing opponent away with feet) and compression (pulling opponent forward with sleeves) cycles. Partner remains relatively passive, allowing guard player to develop timing and feel for off-balancing. Progress to adding sweeps at moment of maximum off-balance.

training_drills.name: Guard Recovery to Double Sleeve
training_drills.description: Start in disadvantaged position (partner standing over you with grips established). Practice recovering to Double Sleeve Guard through grip fighting, hip escape, and foot insertion. Emphasize smooth transition from defensive to offensive positioning.

training_drills.name: Positional Sparring from Double Sleeve
training_drills.description: Guard player starts in Double Sleeve Guard with established grips. Passer attempts to pass guard while guard player works to sweep or submit. Reset to Double Sleeve after any successful pass, sweep, or submission. Focus on maintaining position integrity and recognizing attack opportunities.

expert_insights.danaher: Double Sleeve Guard represents the purest expression of open guard distance management principles. By controlling both sleeves, you neutralize your opponent's primary weapons—their hands—which are essential for establishing grips, controlling your legs, and initiating passing sequences. The position's effectiveness derives from creating a dynamic frame that maintains optimal distance while generating constant off-balancing pressure. The key biomechanical insight is understanding that sleeve control must be paired with active foot placement to create a complete defensive and offensive system. Your feet manage distance and create angles while your hands prevent grip establishment. When these elements work in concert, you create a guard position where the opponent faces constant dilemmas: if they attempt to establish grips, you sweep; if they maintain distance, you transition to more offensive guards like Spider or Lasso. The position teaches fundamental open guard mechanics that transfer to every advanced guard variation.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: In competition, Double Sleeve Guard is your go-to position when you need to slow down aggressive passers and create scoring opportunities. I use it constantly in gi matches to control the pace and set up high-percentage sweeps. The beauty of Double Sleeve is its versatility—you can attack with Scissor Sweeps, Pendulum Sweeps, or transition to Spider Guard depending on how your opponent reacts. The key to making it work at the highest levels is grip fighting aggressively from the start. Don't wait for your opponent to establish their grips first. As soon as you pull guard or open your legs, immediately attack their sleeves and start creating off-balancing pressure with your feet. I particularly like using Double Sleeve against pressure passers because it gives you the control necessary to prevent them from establishing their heavy top game. When they can't get grips, they can't generate the pressure that makes their passing effective. Use this position to frustrate passers and force them into making mistakes you can capitalize on with sweeps.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: Double Sleeve Guard might seem basic, but it's a killer foundation for developing your entire open guard system. In 10th Planet, we look at this position as a gateway to more advanced no-gi concepts because the principles of distance management and off-balancing transfer directly to everything else. Even though we primarily train no-gi, understanding the mechanics of Double Sleeve helps you develop the sensitivity and timing needed for positions like Mission Control or Rubber Guard. The constant push-pull dynamic you create with sleeve control teaches you how to manipulate your opponent's base and create sweeping angles. I tell my students to master the fundamental sweeps from Double Sleeve—Scissor, Pendulum, Flower—because these movements develop the hip mobility and timing you need for everything else. Once you understand how to create momentum and capitalize on your opponent's reactions in Double Sleeve, you can apply those same principles to more innovative positions. It's all about developing that flow state where you're constantly moving, constantly threatening, and never giving your opponent a stable platform to work from.

metadata.title: Double Sleeve Guard Top | BJJ Position Guide | BJJ Graph
metadata.description: Master Double Sleeve Guard Top in BJJ. Complete guide covering passing strategies, grips, and transitions. Systematic passing with 65% success rate.

overview: Double Sleeve Guard Top represents the passing position when facing an opponent who has secured bilateral sleeve grips while on their back. This is one of the most common guard configurations in gi BJJ, where the bottom player controls both of your sleeves at the wrists or forearms to create distance and maintain a defensive barrier. The top player's primary objective is to break these grips systematically while advancing position, requiring excellent grip fighting, posture control, and strategic movement. This position demands patience and technical precision, as rushing against strong sleeve grips often results in sweeps or submission attempts. The key to success lies in understanding grip hierarchy, creating angles to diminish the effectiveness of the sleeve controls, and using strategic pressure combined with grip breaks to advance. Many world-class competitors have built entire passing systems around defeating the double sleeve guard, making it essential knowledge for any serious practitioner. The position serves as a gateway to numerous passing sequences and requires both physical attributes (grip strength, posture) and tactical awareness (timing, angle creation, pressure application).
state_invariants: Top player maintains upright posture with hips elevated above opponent's guard, preventing lower body from being pulled into bottom player's offensive range while maintaining balance through posted hands or controlled grips

Bottom player controls both of top player's sleeves at wrist or forearm level with bilateral grips, creating a frame that maintains distance and prevents top player from achieving dominant grips or closing distance effectively

Bottom player's legs are positioned either with feet on hips, knees bent with shins across, or in dynamic movement patterns to prevent top player from achieving knee cut, leg drag, or other passing entries while maintaining the sleeve control framework

Top player's weight distribution allows for dynamic movement and grip fighting without compromising balance or allowing bottom player to off-balance them with sleeve manipulation or foot placement on hips/biceps
prerequisites: Opponent has established both sleeve grips while maintaining guard position
Top player has achieved standing or combat base posture above the guard
Sufficient distance exists between players due to bottom player's sleeve control and leg positioning
Top player maintains balance and posture despite bilateral sleeve grips
Bottom player is on their back with active guard retention using legs and sleeve controls
key_principles: Maintain strong upright posture with chest forward and hips back to prevent being pulled forward into submissions or sweeps
Systematically break grips using proper grip breaking mechanics rather than relying purely on strength
Create angles and circular movement to diminish the effectiveness of the sleeve grips and create passing opportunities
Control the distance by managing your own sleeve position and preventing bottom player from establishing additional controls
Use strategic pressure and timing to advance grips on opponent's legs, belt, or collar while managing their sleeve controls
Prevent bottom player from establishing foot-on-hip or foot-on-bicep controls which strengthen their guard retention
Transition between different passing approaches based on how bottom player adjusts their leg positioning and sleeve grip depth

counter_transitions.trigger: Opponent attempts to invert or enter deep half guard
Opponent opens guard or loses one sleeve grip
Opponent attempts single leg X-guard entry
Opponent's grips weaken or they attempt to re-guard

decision_tree.condition: If opponent maintains strong double sleeve grips with feet on hips creating maximum distance
If opponent has sleeve grips but legs are in dynamic movement without stable foot placement
If opponent loses one sleeve grip or weakens bilateral control
If opponent attempts to transition to different guard variation or sweep

common_errors.error: Allowing posture to break forward while opponent maintains strong sleeve grips
common_errors.consequence: Creates vulnerability to sweeps, triangles, and omoplatas as your weight shifts forward into their offensive range
common_errors.correction: Maintain upright posture with chest up and hips back, using core engagement to resist forward pulling while systematically addressing grip breaks

common_errors.error: Attempting to pass immediately without addressing the sleeve grips first
common_errors.consequence: Opponent uses sleeve control to redirect your passing momentum, leading to sweeps or guard retention with minimal effort
common_errors.correction: Break at least one sleeve grip before committing to a passing sequence, or use grips and angles that neutralize the sleeve control's effectiveness

common_errors.error: Using only upper body strength to break grips without proper mechanics
common_errors.consequence: Depletes energy rapidly while often failing to break grips of skilled opponents, leaving you exhausted mid-pass attempt
common_errors.correction: Employ proper grip breaking mechanics using hip rotation, stepping patterns, and leverage rather than pure arm strength

common_errors.error: Remaining static in one position allowing opponent to set up their preferred attacks
common_errors.consequence: Bottom player establishes rhythm, finds optimal grip depth, and sets up sweeps or submissions from a stable defensive position
common_errors.correction: Maintain constant motion through angle changes, circling, and pressure variations to prevent opponent from settling into comfortable defensive patterns

common_errors.error: Failing to control distance after breaking grips, allowing opponent to immediately re-establish
common_errors.consequence: Creates a frustrating cycle of grip fighting without making forward progress toward passing
common_errors.correction: After breaking grips, immediately advance your own grips on their legs or belt while controlling distance to prevent re-establishment of sleeve controls

common_errors.error: Ignoring opponent's foot placement on hips or biceps while focusing only on sleeve grips
common_errors.consequence: Even with weak sleeve grips, strong foot frames can maintain distance and facilitate sweeps or guard retention
common_errors.correction: Address both the sleeve grips and leg positioning simultaneously, using strategies that diminish both control mechanisms

expert_insights.danaher: The double sleeve guard represents a fundamental problem in guard passing that must be solved through systematic grip hierarchy understanding. The opponent's sleeve grips create a distance management system that prevents you from achieving dominant controls. Your primary objective is not merely to break these grips through strength, but to render them ineffective through superior positioning and angle creation. The key principle is recognizing that sleeve grips lose their power when you create angles perpendicular to the direction of their pulling force. By circling and creating angular pressure, you force the bottom player to constantly readjust their grips, creating windows of opportunity for passing entries. The biomechanical reality is that wrist-level grips are weaker than elbow-level grips when you rotate your arms internally while stepping to angles. This systematic approach to defeating the double sleeve configuration involves understanding grip strength vectors, positional hierarchy, and the concept of creating passing angles that minimize your opponent's defensive advantages. The practitioner who masters these principles can pass the double sleeve guard with technical precision rather than relying on athletic superiority.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: In competition, the double sleeve guard is one of the most common defensive configurations you'll encounter, especially at higher levels where people understand guard retention. My approach is aggressive and based on overwhelming the grips through constant pressure and movement rather than trying to break them statically. I look to immediately establish my own grips on their pants or belt while accepting their sleeve grips temporarily, then use powerful toreando-style movements to throw their legs side to side. The reality is that strong sleeve grips become much less effective when I'm controlling their leg positioning and creating lateral movement. expert_insights.eddie_bravo: The double sleeve guard is interesting because it's very traditional gi-based defense, but the principles of defeating it apply to no-gi as well when people are trying to maintain distance with wrist control. I'm also a big believer in the stack passing approach from here because when you stack someone properly, their sleeve grips actually work against them by preventing them from creating the space needed for hip escapes. I like to fake the toreando pass to get them thinking about lateral movement, then suddenly change levels and drive forward into a stack. Another 10th Planet principle is using the twister hook or calf slicer threat from certain passing positions, which makes them think about leg entanglement defense rather than maintaining sleeve grips. The creativity comes from mixing traditional passing with leg lock entries—if they're focused on sleeve grips and preventing you from passing, they're often not thinking about you sitting back for a straight ankle or transitioning to 50-50. The modern game requires being unpredictable and multi-dimensional in your passing approaches.
